topic.name: Ivermectin
topic.short_description: Antiparasitic drug being studied for anti-cancer properties

topic.seo_description: Explore ivermectin's potential anti-cancer properties in our comprehensive cancer research guide. Review latest peer-reviewed studies and clinical findings.
topic.seo_intro:
Ivermectin is an antiparasitic medication that has been used for decades to treat parasitic infections in humans and animals. In recent years, researchers have become increasingly interested in exploring whether this well-established drug might have additional anti-cancer properties. Laboratory studies suggest that ivermectin may interfere with cancer cell growth through multiple mechanisms, including effects on cell signaling pathways and potential immune system stimulation. While these early findings are promising, it's important to understand that ivermectin is not an approved cancer treatment, and most research remains in preliminary stages.

The study of ivermectin as an off-label medication for cancer reflects a broader scientific approach to repurposing existing drugs for new therapeutic applications. This strategy can be more efficient than developing entirely new medications, though it requires rigorous clinical validation before any treatment recommendations can be made. Current research is examining ivermectin's effects on various cancer types through both laboratory experiments and observational studies, with researchers carefully evaluating its potential benefits alongside important safety considerations.

On this page, you'll find information about the current state of ivermectin cancer research, including how the drug may work against cancer cells, what the existing evidence shows, and what clinical trials are investigating. This resource is designed to help patients, caregivers, and healthcare providers understand the research landscape. The articles and studies presented below represent the latest peer-reviewed research available on this topic and should be discussed with your medical team.

articles.title: HSP90AB1-Mediated Ubiquitin-Proteasome Degradation of ITGBL1 Promotes Osteosarcoma Progression by Inhibiting Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress-Induced Autophagy.
articles.summary: In osteosarcoma, HSP90AB1 promotes cancer progression by degrading ITGBL1, a protein that suppresses tumor growth, with ivermectin showing potential as a treatment.

articles.title: Disseminated Strongyloidiasis Following Chemoradiotherapy for Lung Cancer in a Patient Living in a Non-endemic Area in Japan.
articles.summary: A lung cancer patient with HTLV-1 developed disseminated strongyloidiasis after chemoradiotherapy, successfully treated with intermittent ivermectin over six months.
